conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples cause cancer is unsupported by the retrieved evidence.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
**Conclusion:** The blanket claim that food-grade wax coatings on apples “cause cancer” is not supported by the retrieved evidence. But the evidence is stronger for regulatory authorization than for a direct, definitive cancer-risk study of every wax formulation.

FDA guidance says fruit/vegetable coating components must be permitted food additives under applicable conditions of use, GRAS substances, prior-sanctioned substances, or otherwise compliant food-contact substances. This means apple coatings are regulated by ingredient and use—not that any arbitrary “wax” is acceptable.  
https://www.fda.gov/regulatory-information/search-fda-guidance-documents/cpg-sec-562550-safety-and-labeling-waxed-coated-fruits-and-vegetables

For carnauba wax—a common glazing wax—U.S. regulation lists it as a direct human-food substance, and identifies its botanical source (Brazilian wax-palm leaves and buds).  
https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-21/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-184/subpart-B/section-184.1978

The most important caveat comes from EFSA’s 2012 re-evaluation of carnauba wax (E903): it reported that **no chronic-toxicity or carcinogenicity studies were available**, said long-term data were lacking, and therefore did not establish an acceptable daily intake. Thus, this review does **not** provide evidence that carnauba wax causes cancer—but it also does not amount to a robust long-term carcinogenicity demonstration of safety.

https://ucrisportal.univie.ac.at/en/publications/scientific-opinion-on-the-re-evaluation-of-carnauba-wax-e-903-as-/

So your view is broadly justified: “apple wax causes cancer” overstates the available evidence. A more accurate statement is that regulated food-grade coatings are authorized for use, while long-term cancer evidence for at least carnauba wax has acknowledged gaps.
